```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(flowCore)
  library(flowWorkspace)
  library(openCyto)
  library(ggcyto)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
})

kOutputDir <- file.path("..", "output", "automated_gating_pbmc")

ReadOutput <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path(kOutputDir, name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop(
      "The analysis output is missing: ", path, "\n",
      "Run scripts/01_automated_gating_pbmc.R first."
    )
  }
  read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
}

OutputImage <- function(name) {
  file.path(kOutputDir, name)
}
```

## What this report does

This report walks through a complete flow cytometry analysis in R. It reads eight
FCS files, applies the compensation matrix that the instrument wrote into them,
transforms the fluorescence channels, and gates every sample with one openCyto
template. It then reports the frequency of each population and the spread of those
frequencies across the eight samples.

The report reads the files that `scripts/01_automated_gating_pbmc.R` wrote. It does
not repeat the analysis. Every number below therefore comes from one run of that
script, and re-rendering the report cannot change a result.

### Why the gate hierarchy is a CSV

The gate hierarchy is in `gating/pbmc_gating_template.csv`. It is not in this
document and it is not in a workspace file.

A gate drawn by hand lives inside a FlowJo workspace. To know what a colleague
did, you open their workspace and look. A template is a text file, so a reviewer
reads it in a pull request, a version control system records who changed a cut
point, and the same file gates the next experiment.

Maecker and colleagues sent pre-stained cells to 15 experienced laboratories.
Local gating gave a mean CV of 20.5 percent and central gating of the same raw
files gave 4 percent [1]. The template is the mechanism that makes central gating
practical, because the analysis moves instead of the analyst.

## The dataset

```{r}
#| label: sample-sheet

sample_sheet <- ReadOutput("sample_sheet.csv")
kable(
  sample_sheet[, c("file_name", "donor", "condition", "well", "stimulated")],
  caption = "The eight files, with the design parsed from the file names."
)
```

The design has two donors and four stimulation conditions. `NS` means not
stimulated and `PI` means stimulated with PMA and ionomycin. The files were
acquired on an LSRII on 18 January 2013 and they come from the FlowJo Basic
Tutorial.

```{r}
#| label: event-counts

event_counts <- ReadOutput("event_counts.csv")
kable(event_counts, caption = "Events acquired per sample.")
```

### The panel

```{r}
#| label: panel

panel <- ReadOutput("panel.csv")
kable(panel, caption = "Detectors and markers. A row with no marker is scatter or time.")
```

Two properties of this panel decide what the analysis can do. There is a viability
dye, so dead cells can be excluded rather than left in. There is `FSC-H` beside
`FSC-A`, so doublets can be excluded. A panel with only `FSC-A` cannot gate
singlets at all, and any doublet then counts as a cell in every population below
it.

## Compensation

Spillover is the light from one fluorochrome that a second detector also reads.
The relationship is linear, so the correction multiplies the measured values by
the inverse of the spillover matrix.

These files carry the matrix in the FCS `$SPILLOVER` keyword, written by the
acquisition software from single stained controls. The analysis reads it and
applies it.

```{r}
#| label: spillover-top

spillover_top <- ReadOutput("spillover_top10.csv")
spillover_top$percent <- round(100 * spillover_top$spill, 2)
kable(
  spillover_top[, c("from", "to", "percent")],
  caption = "The ten largest spillover values, as a percentage.",
  col.names = c("From detector", "Into detector", "Spillover, percent")
)
```

The largest value names the pair of detectors that compensation actually moves.
That pair is the one to inspect on a plot, because an error in the matrix shows
there first.

```{r}
#| label: spillover-matrix

spillover <- as.matrix(read.csv(
  file.path(kOutputDir, "spillover_matrix.csv"),
  row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE
))
kable(
  round(spillover, 3),
  caption = "The full spillover matrix. The diagonal is 1 by construction."
)
```

### Doing this without a stored matrix

When the file carries no matrix, compute one from single stained controls with
`flowStats::spillover_ng()`. In Python the equivalent is a `flowkit.Matrix` built
from the controls. Compensating with a matrix from a different acquisition day is
the common mistake, and it produces a population that does not exist.

## Transformation

Fluorescence data spans several orders of magnitude, and after compensation it
holds negative values. A log transform cannot represent the negative part. The
logicle transform is linear near zero and logarithmic above it, so the negative
population stays visible and the positive population stays separated.

```{r}
#| label: transform-channels

channels <- readLines(file.path(kOutputDir, "transformed_channels.txt"))
cat("Transformed channels:\n")
cat(paste0("  ", channels, collapse = "\n"))
```

One transform is estimated on the first sample and applied to all eight. A per
sample estimate would move a gate between samples for a reason that has nothing to
do with the biology.

## The gating template

```{r}
#| label: template

template <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "pbmc_gating_template.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(
  template[, c("alias", "pop", "parent", "dims", "gating_method")],
  caption = "The gating template. Each row is one population."
)
```

Read the table as a sentence per row. The `nonDebris` row says: from `root`, on
`FSC-A` and `SSC-A`, fit a `flowClust` gate and keep the positive population.

The template fixes the method and the channels. It does not fix the cut point.
openCyto fits every gate on every sample separately, so a sample whose
distribution sits slightly differently still gets its own boundary. That is the
difference between a template and a copied gate.

```{r}
#| label: gating-tree
#| fig-cap: "The gate hierarchy that the template produced."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("gating_tree.png"))
```

## The gates

Each figure shows one gate on the first sample, with the fitted boundary drawn on
the data it was fitted to.

```{r}
#| label: gate-figures
#| results: asis

populations <- readLines(file.path(kOutputDir, "population_paths.txt"))
populations <- setdiff(populations, "root")

for (population in populations) {
  image_name <- paste0(
    "gate_", gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", population), ".png"
  )
  image_path <- OutputImage(image_name)
  if (file.exists(image_path)) {
    cat("\n\n### ", population, "\n\n", sep = "")
    cat("![](", image_path, ")\n\n", sep = "")
  }
}
```

## Results

### Frequency of every population

```{r}
#| label: population-stats

population_stats <- ReadOutput("population_stats.csv")
kable(
  population_stats[, c("sample", "population", "count", "percent_of_parent")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Event count and percentage of the parent population, per sample."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: frequency-plot
#| fig-cap: "Population frequency by condition. One template gated all eight samples."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("population_frequencies.png"))
```

### Spread across the eight samples

This is the number the example exists to produce.

```{r}
#| label: spread

spread <- ReadOutput("population_spread.csv")
kable(
  spread,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation of each population frequency across all eight samples."
)
```

The coefficient of variation here holds the biological difference between two
donors, the difference between four stimulation conditions, and the technical
spread of the assay. It does not hold any analyst variation, because one template
gated every sample.

That last clause is the whole point. Add eight analysts drawing their own gates on
these same eight files and the CV rises, without a single event changing. McNeil
and colleagues measured this directly: 110 laboratories gating one shared set of
files produced 110 different gating approaches, and the standard deviations were
2.5 to 25 times larger under laboratory specific gating than under a consensus
protocol [2].

```{r}
#| label: spread-by-condition

spread_by_condition <- ReadOutput("population_spread_by_condition.csv")
kable(
  spread_by_condition,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The same statistics, split by stimulation condition. Splitting removes the between condition difference from the spread."
)
```

Compare the two tables. The pooled CV mixes the stimulation effect into the
spread. The split CV does not, so it is closer to a measure of the assay itself.

## Reproducing this

```bash
# Pull the dataset, about 207 MB of the 103 GB archive
./sync.sh pull datasets/flowjo

# Build the container. Every package version is pinned and asserted at build time.
./containers/build.sh

# Run the analysis
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  Rscript scripts/01_automated_gating_pbmc.R

# Render this report
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  quarto render reports/automated_gating_pbmc.qmd
```

```{r}
#| label: session-info

sessionInfo()
```
